abstract: Broadly observed trophic scaling patterns relate the biomass of predators to the biomass of prey, and biomass to productivity. The consistency with which these patterns are observed suggests the existence of governing principles that apply across ecosystems. We present a model for the trophic interaction between phytoplankton and zooplankton that produces the scaling patterns as an emergent property of resource enrichment without invoking the influence of phenotypic or genotypic diversity on system structure. Using formulations with broad empirical support, the model incorporates processes that are common to all ecosystems: resource enrichment, feeding, growth, maintenance, and mortality. Thus, our interpretation of widely observed scaling relationships provides constraints for models that quantify the coupling between ecosystem structure and elemental cycles across terrestrial and aquatic environments.
